content: The prevalence of resistance to pyrazinamide (PZA) among cases with rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) was observed to exceed 40%, while resistance to isoniazid (INH) was above 65%. However, resistance to fluoroquinolones (FQs) was below 30%. This highlights the necessity of adopting precise and tailored implementation strategies for any new tuberculosis (TB) diagnostic assays under development. These strategies must consider the variability in resources and needs across different countries, the geographical differences in TB epidemiology and associated comorbidities, the prevalence of drug-resistant TB (DR-TB), and the specialized nature of the technical procedures involved. Although this document does not provide specific guidance on implementation strategies, the characteristics outlined in the Target Product Profile (TPP) should account for the critical steps required to implement and scale up diagnostic tools effectively. The process of updating and consolidating the TPPs builds upon the work conducted during the development of the initial high-priority TPPs for new TB diagnostics. These TPPs are the result of a consultative process involving numerous stakeholders from the global health and scientific communities. The methodology for updating the TPP for next-generation drug susceptibility testing (DST) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis has been published. During the consolidation process, minor editorial changes and reformatting were made, but the technical content of the TPP remained unchanged. Additional processes were employed to develop and update each TPP as needed. For instance, in the current update for a diagnostic test to detect M. tuberculosis in peripheral settings, parameters related to performance and costs were informed by a modeling exercise. The revised TPPs underwent a Delphi-like consultation process, followed by several rounds of feedback and revisions. Draft TPPs were also made available for public comment on the World Health Organization (WHO) website before being finalized, incorporating all feedback gathered throughout the process. A modeling exercise was conducted to evaluate and refine diagnostic accuracy estimates specified in the TPP for a rapid test to detect M. tuberculosis at the peripheral level. This model explored the trade-offs between improved testing accessibility and the variable accuracy of emerging diagnostic tools in healthcare settings in India, Kenya, and South Africa. These countries were selected due to their distinct patient pathways, diagnostic methodologies, and population characteristics, making the modeling globally relevant. Key diagnostic attributes, such as sample type (sputum versus non-sputum), testing site (point-of-care, near-point-of-care, or low-complexity settings), and result turnaround time, were integral components of the model. The baseline scenario traced the patient journey from symptom onset to diagnosis, estimating required patient visits and potential attrition points within the healthcare system. The modeling outputs indicated that novel point-of-care (POC) tests with minimum sensitivities of approximately 70% for non-sputum samples and 78% for sputum samples could achieve comparable or superior case detection rates compared to the current standard of care in each country. For the TPP update on next-generation DST for M. tuberculosis at the peripheral level, WHO convened a group of about 70 experts from 25 countries during a stakeholder consultation in March 2021. These experts included individuals with experience in microbiology, mycobacteriology, molecular biology, health systems, pricing, procurement, and regulation of medical devices, ensuring balanced geographical and gender representation. Infectious disease specialists, TB diagnostics researchers, and civil society representatives also participated to ensure that the perspectives and needs of TB patients and their communities were considered. In compliance with WHO’s standard procedures for declaring and assessing conflicts of interest, all group members disclosed any financial interests, relationships, or activities that could influence their objectivity. No significant conflicts of interest were identified among the members of the Scientific TPP Development Group. A cost-neutral approach was used to formulate various pricing options, starting with a baseline of $8 for sputum-based, low-complexity tests, reflecting currently available options. The analysis aimed to determine threshold pricing for various scenarios to remain cost-neutral, considering that some types of testing would increase the number of tests performed. An aspirational stance was adopted for optimal pricing, envisioning a future where costs for sputum-based, low-complexity tests would be lower. The baseline cost was halved to $4, serving as a starting point for further stratification based on different specimen types and healthcare settings. This approach was not intended to provide a definitive price point but rather to facilitate informed discussions and decision-making. Draft TPP documents were prepared to promote discussion among different stakeholder groups. Between June 9 and July 10, 2023, the draft TPP for a rapid test to detect M. tuberculosis at the peripheral level was shared through a Delphi-like consultation with experts from national TB programs, reference TB laboratories, technical agencies, researchers, implementers, clinicians, funding organizations, industry representatives, and patient advocates. The consultation for the TPP on next-generation DST was conducted from April to May 2019 with a similar audience. An 80% agreement threshold was set to indicate consensus on the proposed characteristics during the Delphi process. Participants were also asked to provide comments supporting their scores, particularly when they disagreed and scored a characteristic at 3 or lower. The outcomes of the Delphi process showed a high level of agreement for most attributes explored in these TPPs. For the TPP on next-generation DST, no initial agreement was reached on the minimal or optimal requirements for certain characteristics, such as the priority of anti-TB agents for testing, the limit of detection for minor variants, and indeterminate results during detection. For the TPP on the rapid test, the most debated points were the pricing of individual tests, the capital costs of the instrument, and the initially proposed minimal time frame for time-to-result. However, consensus was achieved through successive iterations during the updating of these TPPs. Proposed revised versions of the TPPs, incorporating changes made after the respective Delphi-like consultations, were shared online for public comment through the WHO Data Form. The intended audience included TB program managers, laboratory specialists, clinical practitioners, implementers, researchers, civil society representatives, industry representatives, and patient advocates. Comments were analyzed quantitatively and grouped into themes when possible. The results of the public comment process are provided in Annex 1 and Annex 2. A consultation of the Scientific TPP Development Group was organized on September 13–14, 2023. Feedback received through the online public comment process and the outcomes of the Delphi-like consultation were presented during the consultation for each TPP. The discussions involved a detailed analysis of public feedback and proposed revisions. This inclusive approach fostered information sharing, facilitated the exchange of perspectives, and allowed for clarification of various aspects, ensuring a comprehensive and well-informed decision-making process. Changes and suggestions made during the stakeholder consultation were incorporated into the final TPPs presented in Section 3. Diagnostic manufacturers require TPPs early in the development process to be informed of the targets, technical specifications, and diagnostic performance of the products. These parameters are set through a series of processes and stakeholder consensus, keeping in mind the objectives of the TPPs and their feasibility and utility for the end user. Minimal requirements represent the lowest acceptable output for a specific characteristic, while optimal requirements are more aspirational but realistically achievable outputs. Ideally, products should meet all minimal characteristics and as many optimal characteristics as possible.
